title: Shadow Traffic, Canary Rollout, and Progressive Deployment for LLMs

questions.question: What is the right way to order shadow, canary, and A/B testing for an LLM rollout?
options: Skip shadow entirely and go straight from offline evals to a canary rollout with gates
Canary first to gather live signal, then shadow to confirm it offline, then A/B last
Shadow (zero-impact compare), then canary (live traffic progressive with gates), then A/B for distinct alternatives once stability is confirmed
A/B first to pick a winner, then shadow the winner, then canary it into production
questions.explanation: The lesson's sequence is shadow mode first (zero-impact comparison against production), then canary rollout (progressive live traffic with gates), then A/B testing for distinct alternatives once stability is confirmed.

questions.question: Which set of five metrics does the lesson gate canary progressions on?
options: Latency percentiles, cost per request, error/refusal rate, output length distribution, user-feedback rate
GPU temp, fan speed, queue depth, cost, latency — infrastructure signals rather than the lesson's five gates
Accuracy on offline eval only, re-run at each canary step instead of tracking live production signals
Just throughput, aggregated across the whole canary cohort with no other gate
questions.explanation: The lesson lists exactly these five canary gates: latency percentiles (P50/P95/P99), cost per request, error/refusal rate, output length distribution, and user-feedback rate.

questions.question: Roughly how much run-to-run accuracy variance does the lesson cite for identical inputs on LLMs?
options: Under 0.1%, since the lesson treats GPU floating-point behavior as effectively deterministic
Up to about 15%, due to GPU FP non-associativity plus batch-size variance
Identical outputs run-to-run, since the lesson treats sampling at temperature 0 as the production default
Always 50%, a variance the lesson would call far too high to ever call a rollout stable
questions.explanation: The lesson states measured accuracy variation of up to 15% run-to-run on identical eval sets, caused by GPU floating-point non-associativity and batch-size variance, which is why 'stable' means within expected variance rather than identical to baseline.

questions.question: What is shadow mode for, in the lesson's framing?
options: Replacement for rollback, since the lesson treats shadow logs as an alternative to a policy-flag revert
A complete quality test that fully replaces evals, catching every perceptible quality regression before launch
Final production rollout step, run after canary and A/B have already shipped the model to 100%
A smoke test catching cost blow-ups, length regressions, refusal changes, and hard errors — not a quality guarantee
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that shadow mode catches cost blow-ups, length regressions, obvious refusal changes, and hard errors with zero user impact, but does not catch the quality delta users would perceive -- it is a smoke test, not a quality test.

questions.question: What is the correct rollback design per the lesson?
options: Flip a policy flag and revert the pinned model digest in seconds — no redeploy
Wait for the next scheduled release window, since the lesson treats ad-hoc rollback as unsafe
Redeploy with a new model digest, taking hours, since the lesson treats redeploy as the only safe path
Manual SSH to each pod to patch the running model reference one instance at a time
questions.explanation: The lesson's rollback design keeps policy in config/flags and the model in a registry with pinned digests, so rollback is flipping the policy flag and reverting the pinned digest in seconds, not a multi-hour redeploy.

questions.question: Why is cost listed as a gate alongside latency and quality?
options: Cost is automatically capped by every provider, so the lesson treats a dedicated gate as unnecessary
A 20% better model can be 3x more expensive per call; shipping that without a cost gate breaks unit economics
Cost is a vanity metric the lesson tracks for reporting only, not as a rollout gate
Cost is the same across providers, so the lesson treats it as a fixed constant rather than a gate
questions.explanation: The lesson notes cost is a variable, not a constant: a 20% better model can be 3x more expensive per call, so shipping it without a cost gate (breach threshold: >20% above baseline) can break unit economics even though offline accuracy improved.
